chapters.title: In the Prophet's Shadow
comprehension_flags: The abbreviation "bt." in "Fatima bt. Asad" stands for "bint" (daughter of) and a general reader may not recognize it without a gloss this pass is not authorized to add.

chapters.title: The People of the House and the Prophet's Witness
comprehension_flags: The dual date "the year 10/632" uses the Hijri/Gregorian convention, which a general reader may not recognize as two calendars for the same year.

chapters.title: Intellect, Not Reason
comprehension_flags: The terms "apophasis" / "apophatic discourse" (the language of negation) carry the argument of several paragraphs but are never glossed in the source, and a general reader may stumble on them; this pass is not authorized to add an inline explanation.
terminology_notes: signs / ayat — the source renders the same word as Arabic script (آیات) in one place and as a Latin transliteration ("ayat") in another; a book-wide decision on one consistent form would help.

chapters.title: The Discourse to Kumayl
comprehension_flags: The references to "the second chapter" and "the third chapter" assume the reader knows this edition's overall structure; a reader meeting this chapter on its own may not know which chapters are meant.
terminology_notes: 'aqil — the source alternates between "'aqil" and "aqil"; standardized here to "'aqil" throughout, and "'alim rabbani" likewise regularized, for one consistent spelling per term book-wide.

chapters.title: A Sacred Conception of Justice
terminology_notes: Plato's tripartite soul — the source's "concupiscent" and "irascible" were rendered as "appetitive" and "spirited" (paired with "rational") for lucidity; this triad should be standardized book-wide wherever the tripartition recurs.

chapters.title: Justice and the Tyrant's Pride
terminology_notes: fitra — the prose uses "fitra" throughout, while the parenthetical inside the 30:30 quotation reads "firat Allah"; the transliteration should be standardized book-wide, though it sits inside a verbatim quotation and so was left untouched here.

chapters.title: Conscience, Compassion, and the Ordering of Society
terminology_notes: al-nafs al-ammara — the source prints both "al-nafs al-ammara" and "nafs al-ammara" (and once "the soul which commands evil") for the same term; a single form should be settled on book-wide.
su al-zann / su' zannihim bil-baqa — the source romanizes the same root (سوء الظن) two ways; standardize the apostrophe/spelling of this transliteration book-wide.

chapters.title: Justice for the Poor and the Sincerity of Intention
editorial_queries: The source sentence beginning "If one speaks the truth without grasping the reason for it, that truth, الحق, is the very nature of the Creator..." is grammatically broken; it was read as "without grasping the reason for it — namely that الحق is the Creator's nature and that the goal is to take on His qualities," which is the only coherent sense.

chapters.title: Prayer, Remembrance, and Gazing on the Good
comprehension_flags: A general reader may stumble on "supererogatory," which the source uses for voluntary devotions performed beyond the obligatory; the passage pairs it with "voluntary prayer" nearby, but a brief book-wide gloss on first use would help.
terminology_notes: supererogatory — standardize as the book's single term for optional/voluntary acts of worship, rendered identically on every occurrence.

chapters.title: Dhikr: The Polish of the Heart
Remembrance as the Quintessence of Worship
terminology_notes: dhikruLlah / dhikr Allah — the running form is dhikruLlah, but the al-Sadiq quotation prints 'dhikr Allah' (untouched as an artifact); a book-wide pass should confirm the running spelling is consistent throughout.

dhikr / al-haqiqa / tawhid / mazhar / tawajjuh / sultan / khutba — these transliterated technical terms recur throughout and should be rendered identically at every occurrence book-wide, matching the spellings already used here (no diacritics added).

chapters.title: Extinction and the Name: The Death of the Saint
The First Sermon of the Nahj al-Balagha
comprehension_flags: The cosmogonic passage — the winds, the churned waters, and the foam raised into the seven heavens — is deliberately dense and figurative, and a modern reader may lose the thread of what is happening without orienting help this pass is not authorized to add.
